_comment: Texas Essential Knowledge and Skills — Social Studies, Grade 8 (United States History to 1877). Codes and wording transcribed from the official 19 TAC Chapter 113 (§113.20) rule text. Store TEKS in data, never baked into artwork. Districts must confirm exact locally adopted standards/codes.
source: Texas Education Agency — 19 TAC Chapter 113 (Texas Administrative Code). https://tea.texas.gov/about-tea/laws-and-rules/texas-administrative-code/19-tac-chapter-113
verificationNote: Codes and wording transcribed verbatim from the TEA §113.20 rule text (Grade 8, U.S. History) — the standards in effect through the 2025–2026 school year. IMPORTANT TRANSITION: In June 2026 the Texas SBOE adopted revised K–8 social studies TEKS for implementation beginning 2026–2027, and the new sections may renumber Grade 8 codes. Confirm which TEKS version applies to your implementation year against the current 19 TAC Chapter 113 and your district's adopted standards before publishing exact codes. See https://tea.texas.gov/academics/curriculum-standards/teks-review/teks-review-and-revision

transition.implementation: phased-in over the coming years; exact rollout being finalized by TEA/SBOE
transition.note: Grade 8 codes below reflect the §113.20 version in effect through 2025–26. The June 2026 K–8 adoption merges Texas/US/world history into a chronological grades 3–8 sequence, so Grade 8 code numbers will change; the implementation year is still being finalized (reports range from 2026–27 to a later IMRA-driven phase-in). Confirm which TEKS version applies to your school year. When the new TEKS are published in a stable citable form, add a parallel standards file (e.g. teks-grade8-us-2026.json) rather than overwriting this one.

8.1(A).text: identify the major eras and events in U.S. history through 1877, including colonization, revolution, drafting of the Declaration of Independence, creation and ratification of the Constitution, religious revivals such as the Second Great Awakening, early republic, the Age of Jackson, westward expansion, reform movements, sectionalism, Civil War, and Reconstruction, and describe their causes and effects

8.4(A).text: analyze causes of the American Revolution, including the Proclamation of 1763, the Intolerable Acts, the Stamp Act, mercantilism, lack of representation in Parliament, and British economic policies following the French and Indian War

8.4(B).text: explain the roles played by significant individuals during the American Revolution, including Abigail Adams, John Adams, Wentworth Cheswell, Samuel Adams, Mercy Otis Warren, James Armistead, Benjamin Franklin, Bernardo de Gálvez, Crispus Attucks, King George III, Haym Salomon, Patrick Henry, Thomas Jefferson, the Marquis de Lafayette, Thomas Paine, and George Washington

8.29(A).text: differentiate between, locate, and use valid primary and secondary sources such as computer software, databases, media and news services, biographies, interviews, and artifacts to acquire information about the United States

8.29(D).text: identify points of view from the historical context surrounding an event and the frame of reference which influenced the participants

8.29(E).text: support a point of view on a social studies issue or event

8.29(F).text: identify bias in written, oral, and visual material

8.7.text: The student understands how political, economic, and social factors led to the growth of sectionalism and the Civil War — including the roles of the Missouri Compromise, the Compromise of 1850, the Fugitive Slave Act, the Kansas-Nebraska Act, and Dred Scott v. Sandford (knowledge-and-skills statement; confirm exact sub-expectation letters against the current rule)

8.8.text: The student understands individuals, issues, and events of the Civil War — including the central role of slavery as a cause and events such as the election of 1860, secession, and Fort Sumter (knowledge-and-skills statement; confirm exact sub-expectation letters against the current rule)
